A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same neural solver-selection work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original TSP and CVRP experiments, benchmark generalization results, component ablations and unseen-solver experiments in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds algorithm-selection comparisons, encoder cost measurements, larger-scale experiments and node-selection case studies.

M1.justification: The encoders, classification/ranking objectives and four selection strategies are retained. The representative-instance solver features, momentum encoder and transformer in v2 Section 4.3 already appeared in v1 Appendix A.9. Additional candidate solvers extend evaluation without changing the selection procedure.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix A.10 adds a larger-scale synthetic TSP scenario with 500-2000 nodes, extending the earlier synthetic range of 50-500 and benchmark evaluation up to 1002 nodes. The existing TSP/CVRP coverage remains; scheduling is discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's individual solvers, static portfolios and basic manual-feature comparison, v2 Table 5 evaluates a Seiler et al. random-forest selector and salesperson features combined with ranking. Table 9 also compares original and GLOP/UDC-expanded solver pools, although individual scores for the added solvers are not listed. This substantially broadens the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: The original splits, training budgets, decoding settings and model configurations are retained. v2 adds average objective values in Tables 10-11, separates selection and solver inference costs in Table 7, and introduces original-versus-expanded-pool controls in Table 9. The large-scale experiment's precise training and split details are not specified.

E4.justification: v2 adds salesperson-feature versus learned-feature comparisons, encoder computation-versus-quality analysis, larger-scale solver-pool tests, and six node-downsampling case studies (Appendices A.5, A.7, A.10 and A.11). These substantially expand the analyses. The unseen-solver experiment is retained from v1 Appendix A.9, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independently seeded selection models and report means and standard deviations. New comparison tables follow the existing practice. Changes to plotted error-bar values do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1-3 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5, 7 and 9 and objective-value columns in Tables 10-11. For example, the new large-scale comparison reports 2.955% for expanded-pool top-2 selection versus 3.562% for that pool's best individual solver. The top-k plot also has small numerical updates, and the introduction's synthetic-CVRP gain changes from 2.01 to 2.00 percentage points.

T1.justification: The attention, pooling, ranking-loss, solver-contribution and momentum-update equations are retained. Neither version adds a distinct theorem or proof, and the new empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a first general framework for instance-level neural solver selection, exploiting complementary solvers to improve solution quality with limited overhead. The central contributions and headline TSPLIB/CVRPLIB improvements remain unchanged. Additional experiments and the scheduling example support or explain the existing general scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets selected nodes as representing clusters, geometric structures and boundaries, and discusses the hierarchical encoder's training-cost/generalization tradeoff. It also adds default strategy recommendations and a scheduling-adaptation example. The static-solver limitation and imperfect top-1 unseen-solver selection were already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the salesperson package, describes univariate feature selection and random-forest classification, and reports encoder training times. Existing hyperparameters largely move from Section 4.1 to Appendix A.2 unchanged. The repository link remains, while v1's separate statement that code and data accompany supplementary materials is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds Seiler et al., Heins et al., Bai et al. (ZTop), Kwon et al. (MatNet), and He et al. (2025), while removing Lin et al. (2022). It strengthens connections to traditional algorithm selection and distinguishes dynamic portfolios from ZTop's static approach. The overall novelty positioning remains stable; ZTop is discussed rather than separately evaluated.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the presentation: v1 Appendix A.9 becomes main-text Section 4.3, experimental implementation details move into expanded Appendix A.2, and related-work and concluding passages are condensed. It also reorganizes appendix sections, renames OPT to Oracle in the text and tables, and adds impact and acknowledgement sections.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column ICML main text. Figure 1(c) is redrawn, the unseen-solver figure moves into the main text, and new comparison tables and node-selection Figure 6 are added. Complete-result tables gain objective columns and are substantially rearranged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens comparative validation and transparency through traditional-selection baselines, separated encoder costs and larger-scale solver-pool tests. The node-selection examples also help explain the encoder. These provide useful incremental support for v1's already established empirical argument, although unspecified training and split details limit reproducibility of the added large-scale experiment.
